concept.name: Last point of support
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event (LPS) marking the low of a reaction or pullback after a sign of strength, typically a retreat to former resistance-turned-support on diminished spread and volume. It is regarded as a low-risk area to initiate or add to long positions before markup.
concept.intuition: After the breakout rally, the market takes one last quiet step back to the old ceiling, now a floor — the final boarding call for longs.
concept.mechanics: Once an SOS demonstrates demand, subsequent pullbacks are monitored: an LPS holds at or above prior resistance with narrowing spread and shrinking volume, indicating supply is exhausted. Despite the singular name, several LPSs can occur; Wyckoff's point-and-figure counts are conventionally anchored at the LPS level.
relationships: Backup to the edge of the creek
concept.failure_modes: A pullback labeled LPS can fail and re-enter the trading range, invalidating the markup scenario; distinguishing a healthy LPS from the start of a reversal is only possible as subsequent action unfolds.
concept.misconceptions: The LPS is not necessarily the last pullback ever, nor must it touch the exact old resistance; it is a zone defined by diminished volume and spread, not a precise price.
concept.example: After jumping above its 102 range top, a stock pulls back to 103 on half the breakout volume; the trader buys there with a stop below the old range, treating the dip as the LPS.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
